title: Organisation of Data
description: Class 11 Economics: classification of data, discrete and continuous variables, frequency distribution and class intervals (inclusive vs exclusive), and building a frequency table.

topics.title: Classification of Data and Variables
topics.concept:
Once data are collected, they arrive as a confusing heap of raw figures. The next stage of a statistical study is to bring order to this heap — this is the organisation of data. The first step is classification: arranging the data into groups or classes according to their common characteristics, so that comparison and analysis become easy.

Data can be classified on four bases:

  • Geographical — by place or region (e.g. population of different states).
  • Chronological — by time (e.g. India's GDP year by year).
  • Qualitative — by a quality or attribute that cannot be measured in numbers (e.g. people grouped by gender, literacy or religion).
  • Quantitative — by a characteristic that can be measured in numbers (e.g. height, weight, income, marks).

A characteristic that can be measured and takes different numerical values is called a variable. Variables are of two kinds:

  • Discrete variable — takes only whole, separate values, with jumps in between (e.g. the number of children in a family: 0, 1, 2, 3 — never 2.5).
  • Continuous variable — can take any value within a range, including fractions (e.g. height, weight or temperature, which can be 160.5 cm, 55.25 kg, etc.).

Knowing whether a variable is discrete or continuous decides how its frequency table is built.

examples.problem: Example 1: On what four bases can data be classified?
examples.solution:
Data are grouped by a common characteristic.

  • Geographical (place), chronological (time).
  • Qualitative (attribute) and quantitative (measurable).

examples.problem: Example 2: Classify these variables as discrete or continuous: (a) number of cars in a street, (b) weight of students.
examples.solution:
Can the value be a fraction?

  • (a) Number of cars — only whole values — discrete.
  • (b) Weight — can be any value like 48.6 kg — continuous.
examples.answer: (a) Number of cars = discrete; (b) weight of students = continuous.

examples.problem: Example 3: India's wheat output recorded for each year from 2010 to 2020 is classified on which basis?
examples.solution:
It is arranged by time.

  • Year-by-year data are arranged chronologically.

recap:
• Classification = arranging raw data into groups by common characteristics.
  • Bases: geographical (place), chronological (time), qualitative (attribute), quantitative (measurable).
  • Variable = a measurable characteristic with different values.
  • Discrete (whole values only, e.g. number of children) vs continuous (any value in a range, e.g. height).

quiz.q: Arranging India's yearly GDP figures is an example of ____ classification.
The number of children in a family is a:
quiz.explanation: It takes only whole values, so it is a discrete variable.

topics.title: Frequency Distribution and Class Intervals
topics.concept:
When the same value occurs again and again in data, we record how many times it occurs. The number of times a value (or group of values) appears is its frequency, and a table showing values with their frequencies is a frequency distribution.

For a discrete variable we can list each value and its frequency directly. But for a continuous variable, or when the data spread over a wide range, we group the values into class intervals (such as 0–10, 10–20, 20–30). Some key terms:

  • The two ends of a class are its class limits — the smaller is the lower limit, the larger the upper limit.
  • The difference between the upper and lower limit is the class size (width); for 10–20 it is 10.
  • The middle value of a class is its mid-point (class mark) = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2; for 10–20 it is 15.

There are two ways to form class intervals:

  • Inclusive method — both limits are included in the class (e.g. 0–9, 10–19, 20–29). There is a gap between classes, so it suits discrete data.
  • Exclusive method — the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next, and the upper limit is excluded (e.g. 0–10, 10–20: a value of exactly 10 goes into 10–20). This avoids gaps and suits continuous data. An inclusive table can be converted to exclusive form to remove the gaps before drawing graphs.

examples.problem: Example 1: For the class interval 20–30, find the class size and the mid-point.
Example 2: In the exclusive class 10–20, where does a value of exactly 10 go?
examples.solution:
The upper limit is excluded, the lower included.

  • In the exclusive method, 10 belongs to the class 10–20 (not to 0–10).
examples.answer: Into the class 10–20 (the lower limit is included; the upper limit is excluded).

examples.problem: Example 3: Which method (inclusive or exclusive) is better suited to continuous data, and why?
examples.solution:
Continuous data has no gaps.

  • The exclusive method, because it leaves no gap between classes.
  • This matches the continuous nature of the data.
examples.answer: The exclusive method, because it has no gaps between classes, matching continuous data.

recap:
• Frequency = how many times a value occurs; frequency distribution = values with their frequencies.
  • Class interval (e.g. 10–20): class size = upper − lower; mid-point = (lower + upper) ÷ 2.
  • Inclusive (both limits included; gaps; suits discrete) vs exclusive (upper limit excluded; no gaps; suits continuous).

quiz.q: The mid-point (class mark) of the class 40–50 is:
In which method is the upper limit of a class excluded from it?
quiz.explanation: The exclusive method excludes the upper limit, leaving no gaps.

topics.title: Constructing a Frequency Table
topics.concept:
Let us put it all together and build a frequency table from raw data. Suppose 20 students scored the following marks (out of 50):

12, 23, 35, 41, 9, 18, 27, 33, 45, 7, 22, 38, 16, 29, 31, 44, 11, 26, 39, 48

To organise these into a frequency distribution using the exclusive method with a class size of 10, we (1) find the range (highest − lowest = 48 − 7 = 41), (2) decide the classes (0–10, 10–20, …, 40–50), and (3) put a tally mark for each value in its class, then count the tallies to get the frequency:

Marks (class)TallyFrequency
0–10||2
10–20||||4
20–30|||||5
30–40|||||5
40–50||||4
Total20

The total of all frequencies (2 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 20) must equal the number of observations — a quick check that nothing was missed. We have turned a messy list into a neat, readable table. The running total of frequencies down (or up) the table is called the cumulative frequency, which we use later for the median and ogive.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why must the sum of all frequencies equal the number of observations?
examples.solution:
Every observation is counted once.

  • Each value is tallied into exactly one class.
  • So adding all frequencies must give back the total number of observations (here 20).
examples.answer: Because every observation is placed in exactly one class, so the frequencies must add up to the total number of observations.

examples.problem: Example 2: In the table above, how many students scored less than 20 marks?
examples.solution:
Add the first two classes.

  • 0–10 has 2 and 10–20 has 4.
  • 2 + 4 = 6.

It is a running total.

  • Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies down (or up) the table.
examples.answer: The running total of the frequencies (used later for the median and the ogive).

recap:
• Build a frequency table: find the range, choose classes, put tally marks, count to get the frequency.
  • Sum of frequencies must equal the number of observations (a check).
  • Cumulative frequency = running total of frequencies (used for median and ogive).

quiz.q: In a frequency table, the sum of all frequencies must equal the:
quiz.explanation: Every observation is tallied once, so frequencies sum to the number of observations.

quiz.q: The running total of frequencies down a table is the:
quiz.explanation: The running total of frequencies is the cumulative frequency.

questions.q: Arranging raw data into groups by common characteristics is called:
questions.explanation: Classification arranges data into groups by common characteristics.

questions.q: Grouping data by place or region is ____ classification.
questions.explanation: By place/region is geographical classification.

questions.q: Grouping data by time (year by year) is ____ classification.
questions.explanation: By time is chronological classification.

questions.q: Grouping people by literacy (literate/illiterate) is ____ classification.
questions.explanation: By an attribute (literacy) is qualitative classification.

questions.q: A measurable characteristic that takes different values is a:
questions.explanation: Such a characteristic is a variable.

questions.q: The number of members in a family is a ____ variable.
questions.explanation: It takes only whole values — a discrete variable.

questions.q: Height of students is a ____ variable.
questions.explanation: Height can take any value in a range — continuous.

questions.q: The number of times a value occurs is its:
questions.explanation: Frequency is how many times a value occurs.

questions.q: For the class 30–40, the class size is:
questions.explanation: Class size = 40 − 30 = 10.

questions.q: For the class 30–40, the mid-point (class mark) is:
In which method are both class limits included and gaps appear between classes?
questions.explanation: The inclusive method includes both limits and leaves gaps.

questions.q: In the exclusive class 20–30, a value of exactly 20 goes into:
questions.explanation: The lower limit is included, so 20 falls in 20–30.

questions.q: The exclusive method is best suited to ____ data.
questions.explanation: The exclusive method, with no gaps, suits continuous data.

questions.q: In a frequency table, the sum of all frequencies equals the:
questions.explanation: Frequencies add up to the total number of observations.

questions.q: The running total of frequencies is called the ____ frequency.
questions.explanation: The running total is the cumulative frequency.

questions.q: A shoe shop records sizes as 6, 7, 8, 9 (never 7.5). The variable 'shoe size' here is treated as:
questions.explanation: Only whole, separate sizes occur, so it behaves as a discrete variable.

questions.q: To draw a histogram, an inclusive table (0–9, 10–19) is first converted to exclusive form (−0.5–9.5, 9.5–19.5) in order to:
questions.explanation: Histograms need continuous classes, so the gaps of the inclusive method are closed first.

questions.q: If a frequency table of 50 observations has frequencies adding up to 48, it means:
options: Two observations were missed or mis-tallied
questions.explanation: Frequencies must total the number of observations (50); a total of 48 signals an error of two.

questions.q: In a class interval of width 10 with lower limit 60, the upper limit and mid-point are:
questions.explanation: Upper limit = 60 + 10 = 70; mid-point = (60 + 70) ÷ 2 = 65.

questions.q: Classifying data first makes later analysis easier mainly because classification:
options: Turns a confusing heap of figures into ordered groups
questions.explanation: Grouping similar values brings order, so comparison and analysis become straightforward.

questions.q: From the table (0–10:2, 10–20:4, 20–30:5, 30–40:5, 40–50:4), the number scoring 30 or more is:
questions.explanation: 30–40 has 5 and 40–50 has 4, so 5 + 4 = 9 scored 30 or more.

questions.q: Temperature recorded as 36.6°C, 37.2°C, 38.5°C illustrates a ____ variable.
questions.explanation: Temperature can take any fractional value in a range — continuous.

questions.q: Cumulative frequency is especially needed later to calculate the:
options: Median and to draw the ogive
questions.explanation: The running totals (cumulative frequency) are used for the median and the ogive curve.

questions.q: Which classification base would you use to compare the populations of five different states?
questions.explanation: Comparing different places (states) uses geographical classification.

questions.q: A class interval written as 10–20 in the exclusive method actually covers values from:
questions.explanation: Exclusive classes include the lower limit and exclude the upper, i.e. 10 ≤ value < 20.
